Standen","details":"The owner signs one merkle root covering every configuration change across every chain. Each leaf is one chain's atomic batch of calls, redeemable permissionlessly by any relayer against a proof. This collapses a multisig round per administrative call into one round per rollout. The signed digest deliberately omits `chainId` and `verifyingContract` from its EIP-712 domain: a domain pinned to one chain would need one signature per chain, which is the cost this contract exists to remove. `ConfigLeaf.chainId` and `ConfigLeaf.configurator` scope execution instead, so a leaf can only run on the chain and the deployment it was written for. The deployment goes in the leaf rather than in `verifyingContract` because this contract does not sit at the same address everywhere (Tron addresses come from TronBox's transaction-derived `CREATE`), and each chain's leaf can name that chain's instance without splitting the signature. The one-signature property only holds for a plain-key owner, whose ECDSA signature verifies identically on every chain. ERC-1271 validity is chain-local, and a Safe binds `chainid` and its own address into the `SafeMessage` it checks, so a Safe owner needs one signature per chain even at the same address with the same signers. A Tron-native multisig (account permissions) must never be the owner. The contract only sees a codeless address, so it checks roots by ECDSA, and `ecrecover` knows nothing about account permissions: the key the account was created from still recovers to it and can sign any root alone, bypassing the threshold. On Tron, have the multisig hold the roles directly, or give the Configurator a plain-key owner if a single key is the intended model. Authority here is the union of every role this contract holds on its targets. A leaf can call anything, including `transferOwnership` on a target. Rotating this contract's own owner invalidates every root the previous owner signed, so pending rollouts must be re-signed after one.  incorrect accounts, or to contracts that are unable to interact with the
 permission system.

@dev Contract module that helps prevent reentrant calls to a function.
 Inheriting from `ReentrancyGuard` will make the {nonReentrant} modifier
 available, which can be applied to functions to make sure there are no nested
 (reentrant) calls to them.
 Note that because there is a single `nonReentrant` guard, functions marked as
 `nonReentrant` may not call one another. This can be worked around by making
 those functions `private`, and then adding `external` `nonReentrant` entry
 points to them.
 TIP: If EIP-1153 (transient storage) is available on the chain you're deploying at,
 consider using {ReentrancyGuardTransient} instead.
 TIP: If you would like to learn more about reentrancy and alternative ways
 to protect against it, check out our blog post
 https://blog.openzeppelin.com/reentrancy-after-istanbul/[Reentrancy After Istanbul].

 by the {ReentrancyGuardTransient} variant in v6.0.

 The `ecrecover` EVM precompile allows for malleable (non-unique) signatures:
 this function rejects them by requiring the `s` value to be in the lower
 half order, and the `v` value to be either 27 or 28.

 IMPORTANT: `hash` _must_ be the result of a hash operation for the
 verification to be secure: it is possible to craft signatures that
 recover to arbitrary addresses for non-hashed data. A safe way to ensure

@dev Returns true if a `leaf` can be proved to be a part of a Merkle tree
 defined by `root`. For this, a `proof` must be provided, containing
 sibling hashes on the branch from the leaf to the root of the tree. Each
 pair of leaves and each pair of pre-images are assumed to be sorted.
 This version handles proofs in memory with the default hashing function.

@dev Returns the rebuilt hash obtained by traversing a Merkle tree up
 from `leaf` using `proof`. A `proof` is valid if and only if the rebuilt
 hash matches the root of the tree. When processing the proof, the pairs
 of leaves & pre-images are assumed to be sorted.
 This version handles proofs in memory with the default hashing function.

@dev Returns true if the `leaves` can be simultaneously proven to be a part of a Merkle tree defined by
 `root`, according to `proof` and `proofFlags` as described in {processMultiProof}.
 This version handles multiproofs in memory with the default hashing function.
 CAUTION: Not all Merkle trees admit multiproofs. See {processMultiProof} for details.
 NOTE: Consider the case where `root == proof[0] && leaves.length == 0` as it will return `true`.
 The `leaves` must be validated independently. See {processMultiProof}.

@dev Returns the root of a tree reconstructed from `leaves` and sibling nodes in `proof`. The reconstruction
 proceeds by incrementally reconstructing all inner nodes by combining a leaf/inner node with either another
 leaf/inner node or a proof sibling node, depending on whether each `proofFlags` item is true or false
 respectively.
 This version handles multiproofs in memory with the default hashing function.
 CAUTION: Not all Merkle trees admit multiproofs. To use multiproofs, it is sufficient to ensure that: 1) the tree
 is complete (but not necessarily perfect), 2) the leaves to be proven are in the opposite order they are in the
 tree (i.e., as seen from right to left starting at the deepest layer and continuing at the next layer).
 NOTE: The _empty set_ (i.e. the case where `proof.length == 1 && leaves.length == 0`) is considered a no-op,
 and therefore a valid multiproof (i.e. it returns `proof[0]`). Consider disallowing this case if you're not
 validating the leaves elsewhere.

@dev These functions deal with verification of Merkle Tree proofs.
 The tree and the proofs can be generated using our
 https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/merkle-tree[JavaScript library].
 You will find a quickstart guide in the readme.
 WARNING: You should avoid using leaf values that are 64 bytes long prior to
 hashing, or use a hash function other than keccak256 for hashing leaves.
 This is because the concatenation of a sorted pair of internal nodes in
 the Merkle tree could be reinterpreted as a leaf value.
 OpenZeppelin's JavaScript library generates Merkle trees that are safe
 against this attack out of the box.
 IMPORTANT: Consider memory side-effects when using custom hashing functions
 that access memory in an unsafe way.
 NOTE: This library supports proof verification for merkle trees built using
 custom _commutative_ hashing functions (i.e. `H(a, b) == H(b, a)`). Proving
 leaf inclusion in trees built using non-commutative hashing functions requires
 additional logic that is not supported by this library.

@dev `EIP712Domain(string name,string version)`. Both `chainId` and `verifyingContract` are
 omitted so one signature covers every chain; EIP-712 permits any subset of domain fields.

@notice Nonce of the next leaf executable on this chain.
 @dev Sequential rather than a per-leaf executed flag: it fixes the order configuration applies
 in, and makes advancing past a leaf equivalent to cancelling it, so superseded leaves from old
 roots can never be redeemed late. Leaf numbering is an off-chain concern; this is the on-chain
 side of it. Read before building a root.
 Nonces are a play order, not a signing order, so a leaf that cannot execute is unblocked by
 signing a new root holding a leaf at the same nonce. Whichever is played first consumes the
 nonce and strands the other. A leaf must hold at least one call, so the do-nothing leaf is a
 single call with empty calldata to an EOA.
@param _owner Signer of configuration roots
@notice Disabled: renouncing would leave every target this contract administers without an admin.
@notice The digest the owner signs for `_root`.

@title Configurator
 @author Michael Standen
 @notice Owner-of-record for route and adapter administration, redeemable from a single signature.
 @dev The owner signs one merkle root covering every configuration change across every chain. Each
 leaf is one chain's atomic batch of calls, redeemable permissionlessly by any relayer against a
 proof. This collapses a multisig round per administrative call into one round per rollout.
 The signed digest deliberately omits `chainId` and `verifyingContract` from its EIP-712 domain: a
 domain pinned to one chain would need one signature per chain, which is the cost this contract
 exists to remove. `ConfigLeaf.chainId` and `ConfigLeaf.configurator` scope execution instead, so a
 leaf can only run on the chain and the deployment it was written for. The deployment goes in the
 leaf rather than in `verifyingContract` because this contract does not sit at the same address
 everywhere (Tron addresses come from TronBox's transaction-derived `CREATE`), and each chain's
 leaf can name that chain's instance without splitting the signature.
 The one-signature property only holds for a plain-key owner, whose ECDSA signature verifies
 identically on every chain. ERC-1271 validity is chain-local, and a Safe binds `chainid` and its
 own address into the `SafeMessage` it checks, so a Safe owner needs one signature per chain even
 at the same address with the same signers.
 A Tron-native multisig (account permissions) must never be the owner. The contract only sees a
 codeless address, so it checks roots by ECDSA, and `ecrecover` knows nothing about account
 permissions: the key the account was created from still recovers to it and can sign any root
 alone, bypassing the threshold. On Tron, have the multisig hold the roles directly, or give the
 Configurator a plain-key owner if a single key is the intended model.
 Authority here is the union of every role this contract holds on its targets. A leaf can call
 anything, including `transferOwnership` on a target. Rotating this contract's own owner
 invalidates every root the previous owner signed, so pending rollouts must be re-signed after one.
 Rotation is two-step and renouncing is disabled: a mistyped owner or a renounce would strand the
 authority over every target this contract holds, with no way back.
